title: Concurrency Pattern: Pipelines
summary: A **pipeline** is a series of stages connected by channels: each stage is a function that receives from an inbound channel, does work, and sends on an outbound channel. Data streams through the stages concurrently — the key discipline is that each stage closes its own output channel and propagates cancellation so nothing leaks.

subtopics.title: Stages connected by channels
subtopics.explanation: A pipeline stage is a function that takes an inbound <-chan, returns an outbound <-chan, and runs a goroutine that reads, transforms, and writes. Composing stages just means passing one stage's output as the next stage's input. This uniform shape is what makes a pipeline composable from small, reusable pieces.

subtopics.title: Each stage owns and closes its output
subtopics.explanation: The goroutine that sends on a channel is the one that closes it — always with defer close(out) — when its input is exhausted. Downstream stages range over that channel and stop when it closes, propagating completion forward. This sender-closes discipline is how a pipeline terminates cleanly from front to back.

subtopics.title: Streaming concurrency
subtopics.explanation: Stages run at the same time: while stage 2 processes item 1, stage 1 is already producing item 2. Throughput is gated by the slowest stage, and memory stays bounded because only in-flight items occupy channel buffers. Concurrent streaming is the performance payoff a pipeline delivers over a sequential loop.

subtopics.title: Cancellation with a done/ctx channel
subtopics.explanation: If a consumer stops early (error, client disconnect), upstream stages must be told to stop too, or they block forever trying to send. Pass a context (or a done channel) and select on ctx.Done() in every stage's send. Cancellation is what lets a pipeline tear itself down without stranding goroutines.

subtopics.title: Early-exit leaks
subtopics.explanation: The classic pipeline bug: the consumer breaks out of its range early, so the upstream stage blocks forever on a send no one will receive — a goroutine leak. Selecting on ctx.Done() in every send gives stages an exit. Avoiding early-exit leaks is the single most important correctness rule for pipelines.

subtopics.title: Bounded buffers & backpressure
subtopics.explanation: Channels can be buffered to smooth bursty stages, but a buffer only delays backpressure — eventually a slow stage makes upstream block, which is desirable. Keep buffers shallow so overload surfaces rather than piling up in memory. In a pipeline, shallow buffers let a slow stage push back on the fast ones instead of hoarding RAM.

foundations.overview: A pipeline turns a sequence of transformations into a chain of concurrent stages connected by channels. Each stage is a small function: it receives values on an inbound channel, transforms them, and sends them on an outbound channel that it owns and closes when its input runs dry. Because every stage runs in its own goroutine, data streams through the whole chain at once — stage 3 can be working on item 1 while stage 1 produces item 3. The two rules that keep a pipeline correct are: the sender closes its output channel (so downstream knows when to stop), and every stage can be cancelled (so an early-exiting consumer doesn't strand the goroutines upstream of it).
foundations.formalDefinition: A pipeline is a composition of stages, each a goroutine that reads from an inbound channel and writes to an outbound channel it solely owns and closes, with cancellation propagated (typically via context) so all stages terminate when downstream stops consuming.
foundations.whyItMatters: Pipelines are how Go expresses streaming data processing cleanly, with bounded memory and natural backpressure. The cancellation/leak aspects are exactly what senior Go interviews dig into.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an assembly line: each station (stage) takes a part off the inbound conveyor, does one operation, and places it on the outbound conveyor for the next station. All stations work simultaneously, and if the line shuts down, every station must know to stop — otherwise a worker stands there forever holding a part.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Each stage's goroutine blocks on receiving from its input and sending to its output; channel handoffs are the synchronization points. When an input channel is closed and drained, the stage's range ends, its deferred close fires, and the close cascades downstream. A select on ctx.Done() gives the runtime a second wakeup path so a blocked send can be abandoned on cancellation.
foundations.realWorldUsage: ETL (read -> parse -> transform -> write), media processing (decode -> filter -> encode), log/metric ingestion, and any streaming transform where data arrives continuously.
foundations.businessImpact: Streaming through bounded channels processes datasets larger than memory and keeps latency low, avoiding the cost and risk of buffering everything in RAM.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Small single-purpose stages are easy to test, reuse, and reorder; the sender-closes and cancellation conventions make composing them safe and shutdown deterministic.
foundations.performanceImpact: Throughput equals the slowest stage's rate; parallelizing that stage (fan-out) is the lever. Shallow buffers smooth bursts; deep buffers waste memory and hide overload.
commonUseCases: ETL and data-transform streams (read -> map -> filter -> sink)
Bounded-memory processing of huge or unbounded inputs
Composing reusable stage functions into different flows

commonMisconceptions.myth: A stage should close its input channel when it's done reading.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A stage closes its OUTPUT, never its input — the upstream sender owns and closes the input. Closing a channel you receive from violates ownership.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Pipelines buffer everything, so they use lots of memory.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only in-flight items occupy channel buffers; with shallow buffers memory stays bounded regardless of input size — backpressure throttles upstream.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the consumer stops early, the pipeline just ends.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Upstream stages block forever on sends no one receives — a leak. You must propagate cancellation (context/done channel) so they exit.

visualExplorer.title: Data streaming through stages
visualExplorer.caption: gen -> square -> filter, each a goroutine joined by a channel. Each stage closes its own output; closure cascades downstream to end the pipeline.

visualExplorer.title: Leak-safe pipeline shutdown
visualExplorer.caption: How closing and cancellation make a pipeline terminate cleanly.

config.intro: How a pipeline starts, streams, and stops without leaks:

steps.name: Wire the stages
steps.detail: Each stage takes an inbound channel and returns its outbound channel; composing them connects the chain.

steps.name: Stream concurrently
steps.detail: Every stage's goroutine runs at once — item i flows downstream while item i+1 is produced upstream.

steps.name: Source closes first
steps.detail: When the generator finishes, it closes its output; the next stage's range ends and it closes ITS output, cascading down.

steps.name: Or cancel early
steps.detail: If the consumer stops early, it cancels the context; every stage's select on ctx.Done() lets a blocked send abandon and return.

steps.name: All stages exit
steps.detail: Either path ends every stage's goroutine — no stage is left blocked on a send or receive.

interactiveExamples.title: A three-stage pipeline
interactiveExamples.explanation: gen produces numbers, square transforms them, take limits to the first 3. Each stage runs in its own goroutine and closes its own output channel. Notice composition is just nesting the stage calls.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the stage cancellable (fix the leak)
interactiveExamples.explanation: The consumer stops after one value, but `square` keeps trying to send the rest — it blocks forever, leaking. Add a context and select on ctx.Done() in the stage's send so it exits when the consumer cancels.

checkpoints.prompt: Which channel does a pipeline stage close?
options: Its input channel, when done reading
Its output channel, when its input is exhausted
checkpoints.explanation: The sender owns and closes the channel it sends on. A stage closes its OUTPUT (usually via defer close(out)) once its input is drained; it never closes its input, which belongs to the upstream stage.

checkpoints.prompt: The consumer breaks after the first value. Without cancellation, what happens to the upstream stage?
options: The stage blocks forever on its next send — a goroutine leak
checkpoints.explanation: After the consumer breaks, no one receives from out. square blocks forever on `out <- 9`, and so does gen behind it — both goroutines leak. The fix is selecting on ctx.Done() in each send.

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this stage panic with 'close of closed channel' or corrupt the pipeline?
options: It closes `in`, which it doesn't own — the upstream sender owns and closes in
checkpoints.explanation: A stage must never close its input. `in` is owned and closed by the upstream stage; closing it here double-closes (panic) and breaks ownership. Only close the channel you send on — out.

checkpoints.prompt: Make this stage's send cancellable so an early-exiting consumer can't leak it.
checkpoints.explanation: Adding `case <-ctx.Done(): return` gives the blocked send an escape: if the consumer cancels, the stage stops trying to send and returns, running its deferred close and avoiding the leak.

codeLab.title: Build and compose cancellable pipeline stages
codeLab.instructions: Implement two stages: `Gen(ctx, nums...) <-chan int` that streams nums, and `Double(ctx, in) <-chan int` that doubles each value. Both must close their output and exit promptly on ctx cancellation. The harness composes them and also cancels early to assert no leak (channel closes).
hints: Each stage runs a goroutine with `defer close(out)` so its output closes when it returns.
Wrap every send in select { case out <- v: case <-ctx.Done(): return } so cancellation unblocks it.
A stage closes only its OUTPUT; its input is closed by the upstream stage when that stage finishes or is cancelled.

debuggingLab.title: Upstream stages leak when the consumer stops early
debuggingLab.symptom: runtime.NumGoroutine() climbs every request; pprof shows many goroutines stuck on a channel send inside pipeline stages.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: When the consumer breaks at v==2, nothing receives from out anymore. gen's goroutine blocks forever on `out <- 3` because the channel is unbuffered and there's no receiver and no cancellation. The goroutine (and any upstream of it) leaks; under a per-request pattern, leaks accumulate until OOM.
commonMistakes: Sending on a stage's output with no select on a cancellation channel.
Assuming `break` in the consumer cleanly tears down the whole pipeline.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Thread a context into each stage and select on ctx.Done() so a cancelled consumer unblocks upstream sends.

solution.expectedOutput: (gen's goroutine returns on cancel; no leak — NumGoroutine stays flat)

theory.question: What is a Go pipeline and what are the channel-ownership rules that keep it correct?
theory.directAnswer: A pipeline is a chain of stages, each a goroutine that receives on an inbound channel, transforms data, and sends on an outbound channel. The rules: a stage owns and closes only the channel it sends on (sender-closes, via defer close(out)); it never closes its input; and closing cascades downstream, so when the source closes, each stage's range ends and it closes its own output in turn. That cascade is how the whole pipeline terminates.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Composable concurrent stages joined by channels, streaming data end to end.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To process streams with bounded memory and natural backpressure, in small testable units.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each stage ranges over its input; when input closes, the range ends and the deferred close fires, signaling the next stage.

theory.whyImportant: Pipelines are a canonical Go pattern; ownership/closing mistakes cause panics and leaks that interviewers love to probe.
theory.realWorldExample: An ETL flow gen -> parse -> transform -> write, where closing the source cleanly drains and shuts down every downstream stage.

nestedTopics.title: Sender-closes
nestedTopics.explanation: Only the goroutine that sends on a channel closes it; receivers never close, preventing double-close and send-on-closed panics.

nestedTopics.title: Close cascade
nestedTopics.explanation: Closing the source ends the next stage's range, which closes its output, and so on — termination flows downstream automatically.

followUps.question: Why use defer close(out) inside the stage goroutine?
followUps.answer: It guarantees the output closes whenever the goroutine returns — whether the input drained or the stage was cancelled — so downstream always sees a clean end.

followUps.question: What gates a pipeline's throughput?
followUps.answer: The slowest stage; you speed it up by fanning that stage out across multiple goroutines.

theory.question: How do you prevent goroutine leaks when a pipeline consumer stops early?
theory.directAnswer: Give every stage a cancellation path. Thread a context.Context (or an explicit done channel) through the stages and wrap each send in a select: case out <- v / case <-ctx.Done(): return. When the consumer stops early, it cancels the context (often via defer cancel()), which unblocks the pending sends in every upstream stage so they return instead of blocking forever.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Cancellation propagation that lets stages abandon blocked sends.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without it, an upstream stage blocks forever sending to a consumer that left — a leak.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: ctx.Done() is a channel closed on cancel; selecting on it gives a blocked send a second, always-eventually-ready case.

theory.whyImportant: Early-exit leaks are the most common pipeline production bug and a standard interview scenario.
theory.realWorldExample: An HTTP handler streams a pipeline; the client disconnects, the request context is cancelled, and every stage's select on ctx.Done() lets it exit cleanly.

nestedTopics.title: defer cancel()
nestedTopics.explanation: Always defer the cancel from context.WithCancel/Timeout so leaving the consumer (even via return/break) signals upstream.

nestedTopics.title: done channel alternative
nestedTopics.explanation: Pre-context code used a shared `done <-chan struct{}` closed to broadcast cancellation; context generalizes this with deadlines and values.

followUps.question: How do you confirm a pipeline has no leaks in tests?
followUps.answer: Compare runtime.NumGoroutine() before and after, or use go.uber.org/goleak; cancel early in a test and assert the goroutine count returns to baseline.

theory.question: How do you thread error handling through a multi-stage pipeline, and what are the common approaches?
theory.directAnswer: Channels carry only values, so errors need an explicit path. Three idioms dominate: (1) wrap the payload in a struct { Val T; Err error } that flows down the pipeline, and let the sink inspect Err — simple and keeps ordering, but every stage must forward failed items; (2) pass a separate error channel (or an errgroup) that any stage can send to, and have the consumer select on both the data and error channels; (3) use errgroup.WithContext so a stage returning an error cancels the shared context, tearing down the whole pipeline, with g.Wait() surfacing the first error. Choice depends on whether you want to keep processing after an error (result-struct) or fail fast (errgroup/context cancel).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Propagating and surfacing failures across concurrent, channel-connected stages.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A pipeline's data channels have no error slot, so failures would otherwise be silently dropped or panic a stage.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Either carry the error alongside each value, send it on a side channel, or return it from an errgroup goroutine that cancels the pipeline's context.

theory.whyImportant: Real pipelines fail per item and per stage; interviewers probe whether you can surface errors without leaking goroutines or losing the failure.
theory.realWorldExample: An ETL pipeline wraps each row in a Result{Row, Err}; parse errors flow to the sink which logs and skips them, while a fatal DB-connection error uses errgroup to cancel the whole run.

nestedTopics.title: Result-struct pattern
nestedTopics.explanation: Send `struct{ Val T; Err error }` so errors ride the same channel as values, preserving order and letting the sink decide skip vs. abort.

nestedTopics.title: errgroup fail-fast
nestedTopics.explanation: errgroup.WithContext cancels the shared ctx on the first stage error; every stage's select on ctx.Done() then unwinds the pipeline, and g.Wait() returns that error.

followUps.question: Why not just log errors inside each stage and continue?
followUps.answer: It hides failures from the caller and can't stop the pipeline on a fatal error; surfacing errors up (via result struct or errgroup) gives the orchestrator control over skip-vs-abort.

followUps.question: How do you avoid a leak when an error triggers fail-fast?
followUps.answer: The errgroup ctx cancels, and because every stage's send selects on ctx.Done(), upstream stages unblock and return — combine with defer cancel() so nothing is stranded.

theory.question: What is the generator pattern in a Go pipeline, and why is it the idiomatic pipeline source?
theory.directAnswer: A generator is a stage with no input channel — it produces values from a slice, a loop, an io.Reader, or a database cursor and streams them onto its output channel, closing it (defer close(out)) when the source is exhausted. It's the idiomatic pipeline head because it presents any data source as a uniform <-chan T, so downstream stages compose the same way regardless of where data originates, and it enforces the sender-closes rule at the source, which is what lets the close cascade downstream and terminate the whole pipeline. A cancellable generator selects on ctx.Done() around each send so it stops producing when the consumer leaves early.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The source stage that turns an arbitrary input into a channel of values.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Downstream stages need a channel to read; the generator adapts files, slices, cursors, or event streams into that uniform interface.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A goroutine reads from the source, sends each value on out (inside a select with ctx.Done()), and defers close(out) so exhaustion or cancellation cleanly ends the stream.

theory.whyImportant: Every pipeline needs a source; knowing the generator idiom (and making it cancellable) is foundational and frequently asked.
theory.realWorldExample: A log processor's generator scans a file line by line with bufio.Scanner, emitting each line on out and closing it at EOF, so the parse/filter/write stages downstream never care that the source was a file.

nestedTopics.title: Cancellable generator
nestedTopics.explanation: Wrap each send in select { case out <- v: case <-ctx.Done(): return } so a downstream early-exit stops production instead of blocking the generator forever.

nestedTopics.title: Lazy vs. eager
nestedTopics.explanation: The generator produces on demand — it blocks on the send until a downstream stage reads, so it never materializes the whole input in memory, keeping the pipeline bounded.

followUps.question: Why must the generator close its output channel?
followUps.answer: Closing signals end-of-stream to the next stage, whose range then ends and closes its own output — the close cascade that terminates the pipeline starts at the generator.

followUps.question: How does a generator over an unbounded source (e.g., a Kafka topic) terminate?
followUps.answer: It only stops on cancellation — select on ctx.Done() around the send and the source read, so cancelling the context ends production and closes out.

scenario.question: An ingestion service processes a stream through a 4-stage pipeline. Under load, memory grows and latency spikes. How do you diagnose and fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: First find the bottleneck: throughput equals the slowest stage, so a slow stage makes upstream stages block (backpressure) and, if buffers are deep, memory balloons. Profile with pprof to see where goroutines wait and check buffer sizes. Fixes: fan out the slow stage across N workers, keep buffers shallow so backpressure surfaces instead of hoarding memory, and ensure cancellation is wired so dropped work doesn't leak. Validate goroutine count stays flat.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A bottleneck/backpressure problem in a streaming pipeline.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Stages run concurrently but the slowest one paces the whole chain; deep buffers turn the slowdown into memory growth.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Upstream stages block on full output channels (good), but oversized buffers store backlog in RAM (bad) instead of throttling.

scenario.whyImportant: Tuning the slow stage and buffer depth is a classic real-world pipeline performance task.
scenario.realWorldExample: A parse stage was CPU-bound; fanning it out to GOMAXPROCS workers tripled throughput and flattened the memory curve.

nestedTopics.title: Amdahl's law
nestedTopics.explanation: Only the parallelizable, bottleneck stage benefits from fan-out; speedup is capped by the serial parts.

nestedTopics.title: Shallow buffers
nestedTopics.explanation: Small buffers smooth bursts but still let upstream feel backpressure, keeping memory bounded under sustained overload.

followUps.question: Why not just add a huge buffer to the slow stage's input?
followUps.answer: It hides overload and grows memory; the system still can't keep up. Better to fan out the stage and let shallow buffers apply backpressure.

scenario.question: Your HTTP handler streams a response through a pipeline (read -> transform -> encode). When clients disconnect mid-stream, goroutine count climbs steadily. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The disconnect stops the consumer (the response writer), but the pipeline stages don't know: an upstream stage blocks forever on a send no one receives — a per-request goroutine leak that accumulates. Fix it by threading the request context (r.Context(), which is cancelled on disconnect) through every stage and selecting on ctx.Done() around each send, so a cancelled request unblocks and unwinds the whole pipeline. Add defer cancel() if you derive a child context. Verify with a leak test: disconnect early and assert NumGoroutine returns to baseline.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An early-exit leak triggered by client disconnect in a streaming handler.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Returning from the handler (or the writer erroring) doesn't stop the goroutines it launched; they block on sends with no receiver.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: r.Context() cancels on disconnect; if stages select on ctx.Done() they unblock and return, otherwise they strand on the send.

scenario.whyImportant: Client-disconnect leaks in streaming handlers are a common, hard-to-spot production issue that map directly onto the pipeline cancellation rule.
scenario.realWorldExample: A CSV export endpoint leaked one goroutine per aborted download; passing r.Context() into the read and transform stages and selecting on ctx.Done() flattened NumGoroutine.

nestedTopics.title: r.Context() propagation
nestedTopics.explanation: The net/http server cancels the request context when the client goes away; passing it into every stage makes disconnect propagate as cancellation.

nestedTopics.title: goleak in tests
nestedTopics.explanation: go.uber.org/goleak.VerifyNone(t) at the end of a test fails if any pipeline goroutine is still blocked, catching the leak in CI.

followUps.question: Why doesn't the handler returning stop the pipeline goroutines?
followUps.answer: Goroutines aren't owned by the function that spawned them; they only stop when their channel closes or they observe ctx.Done(), so cancellation must be explicit.

followUps.question: Where exactly do you put the ctx.Done() select?
followUps.answer: Around every channel send in every stage (and optionally the receive), since the send to a departed consumer is the blocking point that leaks.

systemDesign.question: Design a bounded, cancellable ETL pipeline in Go that reads records larger than memory, transforms them (with the transform stage parallelized), writes to a sink, surfaces errors, and shuts down without leaks. Lay out the stages and the invariants.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Compose four stages joined by shallow-buffered channels: (1) a generator that streams records from the source (file/cursor) and closes its output at EOF; (2) a parse stage; (3) a transform stage fanned out to N workers (the CPU-bound bottleneck) with the results merged back into one channel; (4) a batched writer sink. Thread one context.Context through every stage so cancellation is uniform, and wrap every send in select with ctx.Done(). Errors ride a Result{Val, Err} struct or an errgroup that cancels the context on a fatal error. Invariants: sender-closes (each stage closes only its output; the merge watcher is the single closer of the merged channel); shallow buffers so a slow sink applies backpressure upstream rather than hoarding memory; bounded fan-out width; and a guaranteed exit for every goroutine (input closed or ctx.Done). Shutdown: on completion the generator closing cascades close down the chain; on failure/deadline, cancel the context and every stage unwinds — NumGoroutine returns to baseline.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A production streaming ETL as a composition of cancellable pipeline stages with a parallelized bottleneck.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Datasets larger than memory demand streaming with bounded buffers, and the slow transform stage must be parallelized without breaking the pipeline's ordering/leak guarantees.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: gen -> parse -> fan-out(transform)/merge -> sink, all sharing one context; close cascades on success, context cancel unwinds on failure, shallow buffers enforce backpressure.

systemDesign.whyImportant: This is the canonical senior design question: compose pipelines, fan-out, and context into one system with explicit backpressure, error, and shutdown semantics.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A nightly data-migration job streams 200M rows: gen reads a cursor, parse validates, transform fans out to GOMAXPROCS workers, and a batching writer flushes every 1k rows; a fatal sink error cancels the context and the whole pipeline stops within seconds with no leaked goroutines.

nestedTopics.title: Bottleneck fan-out
nestedTopics.explanation: Only the slow stage (transform) is fanned out; per Amdahl the pipeline's throughput is capped by it, so parallelizing it gives the biggest win while other stages stay single-goroutine.

nestedTopics.title: Backpressure via shallow buffers
nestedTopics.explanation: Small inter-stage buffers let a slow sink push back through the merge and transform to the generator, keeping memory flat under sustained overload.

nestedTopics.title: Ordering across fan-out
nestedTopics.explanation: If the sink needs source order, tag records with a sequence number before fan-out and reassemble at the sink; otherwise document that order is not preserved.

followUps.question: How do you keep memory bounded when the sink is slower than the source?
followUps.answer: Shallow buffers make the merge block on the full sink channel, which blocks the transform workers, which blocks the generator — backpressure throttles the source instead of buffering the backlog in RAM.

followUps.question: Where does the single-closer principle apply in this design?
followUps.answer: At the merge after fan-out: forwarders only send and Done, and one watcher closes the merged channel after wg.Wait(); every other stage closes only its own single output.

coding.question: Implement a cancellable filter stage: `func Filter(ctx context.Context, in <-chan int, keep func(int) bool) <-chan int` that streams only values for which keep is true and exits promptly on cancellation.
coding.thoughtProcess: Run a goroutine that ranges over in and, for each value passing keep, sends it on out. Wrap the send in a select with ctx.Done() so an early-exiting consumer can't block us. defer close(out) guarantees the output closes whether the input drains or we're cancelled. We close only out, never in.
coding.lineByLine: The goroutine defers close(out) so the output is closed on every return path. It ranges over in, which ends naturally when the upstream closes in. For each value, keep decides whether to forward it; dropped values just continue. The kept value is sent inside a select that also watches ctx.Done(), so if the consumer cancels while we're blocked on the send, we return immediately — closing out via the defer and leaking nothing. We never close in; that belongs to the upstream stage.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the channel (streaming, bounded memory).

alternativeApproaches.title: done channel instead of context
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Replace ctx with a `done <-chan struct{}` and select on `<-done`; functionally similar but without deadlines/values that context provides.

alternativeApproaches.title: Generic stage
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Make Filter[T any](ctx, in <-chan T, keep func(T) bool) <-chan T with type parameters so it works for any element type.

followUps.question: Why select on ctx.Done() only around the send, not the receive?
followUps.answer: The receive (`range in`) already unblocks when in closes; the risky blocking point is the send to a consumer that may have left, so that's where cancellation is needed. You can also add it to the receive for symmetry.

followUps.question: What guarantees out is always closed?
followUps.answer: defer close(out) runs on every return path — normal drain or cancellation — so downstream always sees termination.

coding.question: Build a 3-stage pipeline gen -> filter(odd) -> square using a `done` channel for cancellation, and show that breaking out of the consumer early doesn't leak any goroutine. Implement `func Pipeline(done <-chan struct{}, nums ...int) <-chan int`.
coding.thoughtProcess: Write each stage as a func taking done plus its input and returning its output, with defer close(out) and every send wrapped in select { case out <- v: case <-done: return }. gen streams nums, filter forwards only odd values, square squares them. Compose by nesting. When the consumer closes done (via defer close(done) after an early break), each stage's blocked send takes the done case and returns, running its deferred close — no stage is stranded.
coding.lineByLine: Each stage runs a goroutine that defers close(out), so its output closes on any return path. gen streams the inputs, selecting on done so a cancelled consumer unblocks its send. filterOdd ranges its input, drops even values with continue, and forwards odd ones through the same done-guarded select. square squares each value likewise. Pipeline nests them so gen's output feeds filterOdd, whose output feeds square. When the caller closes done (typically via defer close(done) after an early break in the consumer's range), any stage blocked on a send takes the <-done case, returns, and its deferred close fires — the close also cascades so downstream ranges end. Because every send has a done escape and every goroutine returns, no goroutine leaks on early exit.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the channels — streaming, bounded memory.

alternativeApproaches.title: context instead of done
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Swap done <-chan struct{} for ctx context.Context and select on ctx.Done(); adds deadlines and integrates with request-scoped cancellation.

alternativeApproaches.title: Generic stages
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Define stages as func[T,U any](done <-chan struct{}, in <-chan T, f func(T)(U,bool)) <-chan U so filter and map collapse into one reusable, type-parameterized stage.

followUps.question: How would a caller use this and guarantee no leak on early break?
followUps.answer: done := make(chan struct{}); defer close(done); then range Pipeline(done, ...) and break when done — the deferred close(done) unblocks every stage as the consumer returns.

followUps.question: Why is the done channel closed rather than sent to?
followUps.answer: Closing broadcasts to all receivers at once (every <-done unblocks), whereas a send would reach only one goroutine; a broadcast is exactly what cancelling all stages needs.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Build small, single-purpose stages with the signature func(ctx, in <-chan T, ...) <-chan U, each owning and closing its output. Compose by nesting; thread one context through the whole chain so cancellation is uniform. Keep stages stateless where possible for easy reuse and testing.
productionDeepDive.performance: Throughput equals the slowest stage — profile to find it, then fan that stage out across workers. Use shallow buffers to smooth bursts; avoid deep buffers that convert overload into memory growth. Batch tiny items if per-item channel handoff overhead dominates.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Honor sender-closes (only the producer closes a channel) and never close an input. Wrap every send in select with ctx.Done() so cancellation unblocks it. Run -race; pipelines mix many goroutines and shared closures.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always provide a cancellation path so an early-exiting or failed consumer can't strand upstream stages. Defer close(out) so the output closes on every exit. Recover panics inside stages so one bad item doesn't crash the pipeline, and surface stage errors via a separate error channel or errgroup.
productionDeepDive.observability: Export per-stage throughput, queue depth (len of each channel), and runtime.NumGoroutine(); a monotonically rising goroutine count signals a stage stuck on a send (missing cancellation). Use pprof goroutine profiles to pinpoint the blocked send line.
productionDeepDive.security: Bound concurrency and buffer sizes so adversarial input volume can't be turned into unbounded memory or goroutines (a DoS vector). Apply context deadlines so a malicious slow producer/consumer can't hold a stage open indefinitely.

caseStudies.problem: Demonstrate composable concurrent stages without leaks.
caseStudies.solution: Stages that close their output plus a shared done/context channel selected on every send.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A little boilerplate per stage for guaranteed leak-free shutdown.
caseStudies.lessons: Cancellation must be designed in, not bolted on; the sender-closes rule is non-negotiable.

caseStudies.problem: Process datasets larger than memory with low latency.
caseStudies.solution: Bounded-buffer pipelines with the slow transform stage fanned out.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Lost ordering across the fanned-out stage in exchange for throughput.
caseStudies.lessons: Shallow buffers + fan-out on the bottleneck keep memory flat and latency low.

keyTakeaways: A pipeline is a chain of stages joined by channels; each stage receives, transforms, and sends, running concurrently for streaming, bounded-memory processing.
Sender-closes: a stage closes only its OUTPUT (defer close(out)) when its input drains; closing cascades downstream to terminate the pipeline.
Prevent early-exit leaks by threading a context through every stage and selecting on ctx.Done() around each send, with defer cancel() on the consumer side.
Throughput is gated by the slowest stage — fan it out — and buffers should stay shallow so backpressure surfaces instead of hoarding memory.
